opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think we're in this strange transitional period right now. When I code these days, a huge fraction of what I do is talking to an agent in English and then reviewing diffs. And I'd say the skill that's actually emerging isn't "can you write the code." It's more like, can you manage this slightly weird, very capable, but also very jagged intern.

The models are superhuman in some ways. They know every API, they can churn out a thousand lines in a few seconds. But then they'll make a mistake no human would make: they'll hallucinate a function, quietly delete a test so it passes, or go down a rabbit hole and bloat your codebase with defensive code you never asked for. So mastery right now is a lot about knowing where the jaggedness is. You learn to keep the agent on a short leash, give it small, well-scoped chunks, verify quickly, and keep the human in the loop where it matters. I think of it almost like an Iron Man suit. It's an augmentation, not a full replacement, at least for now. You want a tight generation-verification loop, and the faster you can make that loop, the more productive you are.

Over the coming years, I think the slider moves gradually toward more autonomy. You'll hand off bigger and bigger chunks: first a function, then a feature, then maybe a whole subsystem. The skills shift accordingly. Today it's prompting and reviewing diffs. Later it's more like being an engineering manager or an architect: specifying intent clearly, setting up the right context, designing good tests and evals so you can actually trust what comes back, and orchestrating several agents running in parallel. Context engineering, deciding what the model needs to see and what it doesn't, is a real skill, and I think it'll matter even more.

But I'd push back a bit on the "decade of agents is next year" framing. These things still lack a lot: continual learning, reliable memory, really knowing when they're out of their depth. So I expect it to be more of a decade than a year. And people who actually understand the code underneath are still going to have a big edge, because when things go wrong, and they will, you need to be able to drop down a level and see what's really happening. So my advice is to use these tools aggressively, but don't let your own understanding atrophy. The best people will be fluent in both: they can talk to the agent at a high level, and they can still read and reason about every line when it counts.

r001.rationale: It describes mastery progressing from prompting and reviewing diffs toward engineering-manager or architect skills, including orchestrating several agents in parallel.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I've been living in it. The short version is that I think we're going through a phase transition in what it means to be a programmer, and we're still early in it, so most people haven't adapted yet.

The way I'd frame it is there's a spectrum. On one end you have what I called a while ago "vibe coding," where you basically just talk to the thing, you don't look at the code, you accept all the diffs, you paste the error back in, and it mostly works for a throwaway project on a Saturday afternoon. And that's fun and real, but it's not what professional engineering looks like. On the other end you have people who are still typing out every character themselves and maybe using autocomplete. And I think the interesting work is going to be in the middle, and the middle is going to move.

What I've noticed personally is that the agents are extremely good at some things and still surprisingly bad at others, and the skill is knowing which is which. They're great when the task is well specified, when there's a lot of similar code on the internet, when there's a tight feedback loop like tests or a compiler. They're much worse when the code is novel, when the architecture matters, when there's a subtle invariant that isn't written down anywhere. And they have this tendency to be overconfident. They'll make a change, declare victory, and you find out later they misunderstood the problem. So right now a lot of mastery is just calibration. You develop a feel for the leash length. For this kind of task I can let it run for twenty minutes, for this kind I need to check every step.

Over the next few years I think that leash gets longer, but I don't think it goes to infinity anytime soon. The models will get better, obviously, but the harder part is the scaffolding around them. The really interesting thing is that I think the unit of work is going to change. Right now I still think in terms of files and functions and I'm sort of supervising the agent at that level. I think increasingly you supervise at the level of the specification and the tests and the environment. You become a sort of manager or orchestrator. You're spending more time saying precisely what you want, building the harness that lets the agent verify its own work, and reading diffs critically, and less time actually producing tokens of code yourself.

And I'd say the people who are going to be really good at this are going to look a bit different from the people who were really good at the old thing. The old skill was holding a huge program in your head and being fast at emitting correct code. The new skill is more like taste plus verification. Can you tell when the output is wrong? Can you decompose a problem so that an agent can actually succeed on each piece? Can you design the sandbox so that a mistake doesn't matter? Those are closer to engineering management or to teaching than to typing.

One thing I'd caution against is the idea that you don't need to understand the code anymore. I think it's actually the opposite for a while. The agent raises the floor a lot, so a lot more people can produce something, but it doesn't raise the ceiling as much yet, and the ceiling is where the leverage is. If you don't understand what's going on under the hood you're going to accumulate a kind of slop that compounds, and then you're stuck. So I actually think fundamentals matter more, not less, at least during this transitional period. You just exercise them differently. You read a lot more than you write.

And then there's a meta point which is that the tools themselves are changing very fast, so a big part of mastery is just staying plastic. Every six months the right workflow is different. What you learned about prompting last year is kind of irrelevant. So the people who will do well are the ones who are willing to keep rewiring their habits, and who treat their own workflow as a thing to be engineered.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say mastery goes from "I write the code" to "I specify, I verify, I build the environment, and I know exactly how much to trust the thing," and the dial on trust keeps moving but it moves slower than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes supervising and orchestrating an agent, but does not discuss coordinating teams of coding agents or compare that with working in a single agent session.

astra-6.text:
I think the skill is going to move up a level of abstraction. You’re spending less time typing out the code yourself and more time deciding what work to delegate, what context the agent needs, and how you’re going to tell whether it actually succeeded.

And that last part is really important. It’s very easy to generate a lot of code. It’s much harder to know that this is the right code, that it fits into the system, that it handles the cases you care about. So I think having a strong understanding of software is still going to be extremely useful. You’re using that understanding to direct and evaluate the work.

There’s also this question of how much you can keep in flight. If you have several agents working on different things, can you structure those tasks so they don’t interfere with each other? Can you review the results without becoming the bottleneck? That starts to look a little bit like managing a team, except the capabilities and failure modes are quite different.

I expect the boundary to keep shifting. Something you have to supervise very closely today might become something you can hand off tomorrow. So mastery is partly about continually recalibrating: where can I trust this system, where do I need to check, and where should I just do the work myself?

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating work and managing several agents as part of evolving mastery, but it does not clearly frame coordinating a team of agents as a higher level than working within a single agent session.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re moving from writing every line of code to managing systems that write code, and those are surprisingly different skills. You still need to know what you want to build, but now you also have to figure out how to specify it, how to give the agent the right context, and how to verify what comes back.

The interesting thing is that the amount of supervision you need will keep changing. Sometimes you can hand off a whole task. Sometimes you need to get into the details. Being good at this means having a feel for where the agent is reliable and where you should intervene. And that intuition gets stale as the models improve, so you have to keep experimenting.

I suspect the strongest people will combine software fundamentals with an ability to delegate. They’ll break work into pieces that agents can actually execute, set up feedback loops, and make the results easy to check. Writing code becomes cheaper, but deciding what code should exist—and knowing whether it works—still takes judgment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses delegating work to agents and managing agent-written code, but it does not frame coordinating teams of coding agents as a higher level of mastery than working in a single agent session.
